question: The first McDonald's in the UK opened, in Woolwich, south-east London.
explainer: A Big Mac in Woolwich. Britain's high streets would never be quite the same.

question: Rupert Murdoch bought The Sun newspaper.
explainer: He relaunched it as a tabloid within weeks. The rest is very loud history.

question: Paul McCartney and Wings went to number one with "Mull of Kintyre".
explainer: Bagpipes, a Scottish peninsula, and the first UK single to sell two million copies.

question: Castlemaine XXXX lager was first introduced to the UK.
explainer: Brewed here under licence, and sold on the idea that Australians wouldn't give a XXXX for anything else.

question: Back to the Future was released in British cinemas.
explainer: Marty McFly, a DeLorean, and 1.21 gigawatts. Great Scott!

question: Michael Owen scored a wonder goal against Argentina at the World Cup.
explainer: An eighteen-year-old, half the length of the pitch, and a nation on its feet.

question: "Bend It Like Beckham" scored a surprise box-office hit.
explainer: Football, family and freedom, in a Hounslow back garden.

question: Amazon.co.uk opened for business, selling only books.
explainer: Just books to begin with. Then, eventually, absolutely everything.

question: Wet Wet Wet's "Love Is All Around" spent 15 weeks at number one.
explainer: From Four Weddings and a Funeral. They deleted it themselves to make it stop.

question: Tesco launched its Clubcard loyalty scheme.
explainer: Points for your shopping, and a lot of data for Tesco. Everybody won. Sort of.

question: Michael Jackson released the album "Thriller".
explainer: The best-selling album of all time, and a zombie dance routine.

question: Emma Raducanu won the US Open as a qualifier, without dropping a set.
explainer: Eighteen years old, ranked outside the top 100, and a fairy tale in New York.

question: Joe Dolce's "Shaddap You Face" kept Ultravox's "Vienna" off number one.
explainer: Midge Ure has never quite got over it. Understandably.

question: Paula Radcliffe set a women's marathon world record that stood for 16 years.
explainer: London, two hours fifteen, and miles clear of everyone else.

question: The Nescafé Gold Blend couple began their will-they-won't-they adverts.
explainer: A soap opera in forty-second chunks, all over a jar of coffee.

question: Lilt, with its 'totally tropical taste', was launched.
explainer: Pineapple and grapefruit in a can, all the way from... Coca-Cola.

question: Gerry and the Pacemakers took "You'll Never Walk Alone" to number one.
explainer: A Merseybeat cover that became football's most stirring anthem.

question: Sky Television launched, beaming four channels to dishes across Britain.
explainer: Squarials, Sky One, and grumbling about dishes on the front of houses.

question: "Blind Date" first aired, with Cilla Black.
explainer: 'A lorra lorra laughs.' And quite a few awkward holidays.

question: Anita Roddick opened the first Body Shop, in Brighton.
explainer: Refillable bottles and no animal testing, long before anyone else bothered.

question: "Educating Rita", with Michael Caine and Julie Walters, was released.
explainer: A weary tutor, a Liverpudlian hairdresser, and Willy Russell's wit.

question: Viz comic was first published, in Newcastle.
explainer: Roger Mellie, the Fat Slags and Sid the Sexist. Never knowingly tasteful.

question: "Top of the Pops" was first broadcast.
explainer: Chart hits, dodgy miming, and a Thursday-night ritual for decades.

question: The Sony PlayStation went on sale in the UK.
explainer: Wipeout, Tomb Raider, and the console that made gaming cool for grown-ups.

question: "Peep Show" first aired on Channel 4.
explainer: Mark and Jeremy, filmed from the inside of their heads.

question: Red Bull went on sale in the UK.
explainer: It gives you wings, apparently. Also, a slight twitch.

question: Bonnie Tyler reached number one with "Total Eclipse of the Heart".
explainer: Turn around, bright eyes. Welsh gravel and Wagnerian drama.

question: "Have I Got News For You" first aired.
explainer: Satire with Ian Hislop and Paul Merton. Plus a tub of lard, once.

question: BBC iPlayer launched.
explainer: No more setting the video. Catch-up TV went mainstream.

question: New Order released "Blue Monday", the best-selling 12-inch single ever.
explainer: The elaborate sleeve cost so much they lost money on every copy sold.

question: "Bullseye" first aired, with Jim Bowen.
explainer: 'Look at what you could have won.' Usually a speedboat.

question: The Premier League kicked off its very first season.
explainer: Sky's money, Monday Night Football, and the game changed forever.

question: The Raleigh Chopper bike was launched in Britain.
explainer: High-rise handlebars, a gearstick between your legs. Health and safety looked away.

question: Guinness's 'Surfer' advert, with its galloping white horses, first aired.
explainer: Tick follows tock follows tick. Regularly voted the best advert ever made.

question: "Ghostbusters" was released.
explainer: Who you gonna call? Everybody knew the answer.

question: "Thunderbirds", Gerry Anderson's Supermarionation series, launched.
explainer: F.A.B. Puppets, strings, exploding models, and International Rescue.

question: "The Young Ones", the anarchic student sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Rick, Vyvyan, Neil and Mike, and the birth of alternative comedy.

question: Spotify launched in the UK.
explainer: All the music in the world, and the slow death of the CD rack.

question: "Top Gun" was released.
explainer: Aviators, volleyball, and a need for speed.

question: "Neighbours" was first shown on BBC One.
explainer: Ramsay Street at lunchtime, and again at teatime for those who missed it.

question: easyJet's first flight took off, from Luton to Glasgow.
explainer: Tickets 'as cheap as a pair of jeans'. Orange everything.

question: Blackburn Rovers, bankrolled by Jack Walker, won the Premier League.
explainer: Shearer, Sutton and small-town Lancashire, briefly on top of England.

question: Rupert Murdoch bought The Times.
explainer: The Thunderer joined The Sun in the same stable. Not everyone was thrilled.

question: "Last of the Summer Wine", the world's longest-running sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Three old Yorkshiremen, a tin bath, and a very steep hill.

question: lastminute.com was founded by Martha Lane Fox and Brent Hoberman.
explainer: The poster child of the dotcom boom, selling holidays and theatre tickets.

question: Del Boy fell through the bar in "Only Fools and Horses".
explainer: A lean on the bar, a perfectly timed fall. Possibly the most repeated moment in British comedy.

question: The iPhone went on sale in the UK, exclusively on O2.
explainer: Touchscreens, apps, and nobody looking up from their phone ever again.

question: Oasis released "Wonderwall".
explainer: Every busker's favourite. Still played at every party you've ever been to.

question: "Dallas" viewers finally found out who shot J.R.
explainer: It was Kristin. The whole country stayed in to find out.

question: Tate Modern opened in the old Bankside power station on the Thames.
explainer: A vast turbine hall, and modern art for the millions.

question: Coca-Cola's 'Holidays are coming' lorries first appeared on British TV.
explainer: The unofficial start of Christmas for a whole generation.

question: "Notting Hill", the Richard Curtis romantic comedy, was released.
explainer: A travel bookshop, a film star, and 'just a girl, standing in front of a boy'.

question: Rage Against the Machine beat The X Factor to the Christmas number one.
explainer: A Facebook campaign against Simon Cowell, and it actually worked.

question: Starbucks arrived in Britain by buying the Seattle Coffee Company.
explainer: Lattes to go, and your name spelt wrong on the cup, from then on.

question: André Previn joined Morecambe and Wise, playing 'all the right notes'.
explainer: 'But not necessarily in the right order.' Christmas TV gold.

question: Ed Sheeran released "Shape of You".
explainer: Streamed into the billions. And played in every gym in the land.

question: Cadbury's Wispa went on sale across the whole country.
explainer: All those bubbles. Axed, then brought back by a Facebook campaign.

question: "Love Actually" was released.
explainer: Billy Mack, Hugh Grant's dancing PM, and those cue cards.

question: The new Wembley Stadium opened, with its giant arch.
explainer: Years late, wildly over budget, and well worth the wait. Mostly.

question: The Guinness Book of Records was first published.
explainer: Born from a pub argument about Europe's fastest game bird.

question: "Jaws" was released, and people were scared to go back in the water.
explainer: Da dum. Da dum. The first summer blockbuster.

question: Monster Munch crisps were launched.
explainer: Originally called The Prime Monster. Pickled onion was, and is, the correct flavour.

question: Kim Wilde released "Kids in America".
explainer: New Wave pop out of Hertfordshire, conquering the airwaves.

question: The Animals released "The House of the Rising Sun".
explainer: A Newcastle band, an old American folk tune, and a haunting organ.

question: The 'You know when you've been Tango'd' advert first aired.
explainer: An orange man slapping people. Pulled after playground copycats.

question: Daniel Craig made his James Bond debut in "Casino Royale".
explainer: Blond Bond, those blue trunks, and some very sceptical critics proved wrong.

question: Apple launched the very first iPod.
explainer: A thousand songs in your pocket, and white earphones everywhere.

question: The National Lottery held its very first draw.
explainer: Mystic Meg, a giant pointing finger, and 'It could be you'.

question: Ceefax, the BBC's teletext service, was launched.
explainer: Page 302 for the football scores, while the jazz played.

question: Netflix launched its streaming service in the UK.
explainer: Binge-watching was about to become a national pastime.

question: "Grange Hill", the gritty comprehensive-school drama, first rang its bell.
explainer: School life with all the warts, and sausages on forks, left in.

question: The first Glastonbury Festival took place, at Worthy Farm.
explainer: Tickets cost £1, and that included free milk from the farm.

question: "The Wicker Man", the great British folk-horror, was released.
explainer: A remote Scottish isle, pagan rites, and a genuinely alarming ending.

question: "The Royle Family" first aired.
explainer: A family, a sofa, a telly. 'My arse!'

question: Cadbury's drumming gorilla advert first aired.
explainer: Phil Collins, 'In the Air Tonight', and a gorilla who really, really meant it.

question: ABBA won Eurovision with "Waterloo", in Brighton.
explainer: Glitter, platform boots, and four Swedes on the way to world domination.

question: "Absolutely Fabulous" first aired, with Edina and Patsy behaving very badly.
explainer: Sweetie darling, endless Bolly, and the funniest excess on television.

question: Marathon bars were renamed Snickers in the UK.
explainer: Same peanuts, new name, and decades of people still calling it a Marathon.

question: Dr. Martens made their first 1460 boot, in Northamptonshire.
explainer: Named after its birthday: the first of April. From postmen to punks.

question: "Gavin & Stacey" first aired.
explainer: Essex meets Barry Island. 'Oh, what's occurring?'

question: Liverpool came from 3-0 down to win the Champions League in Istanbul.
explainer: Half-time at 3-0, and somehow champions by the end of the night.

question: Dizzee Rascal's "Boy in da Corner" won the Mercury Prize.
explainer: East London grime, aged nineteen, and a genuine game-changer.

question: Ridley Scott's Hovis 'boy on the bike' advert first aired.
explainer: Dvorak, a cobbled hill in Shaftesbury, and a loaf in a basket.

question: "Big Brother" first aired in the UK.
explainer: Nasty Nick, a house full of cameras, and reality TV took over.

question: Pirate station Radio Caroline first broadcast from a ship in the North Sea.
explainer: Pop music the BBC wouldn't play, from international waters.

question: The first Penguin paperbacks went on sale for sixpence each.
explainer: Proper books at cigarette prices. Reading, for absolutely everyone.

question: The Range Rover was launched.
explainer: A luxury car that could go up a muddy hill. Chelsea's farmers rejoiced.

question: Ford launched the Cortina.
explainer: Britain's best-selling car for years. The sales rep's chariot.

question: Comic Relief held its very first Red Nose Day.
explainer: Red noses on cars, people, and occasionally on lorries.

question: The Independent newspaper was launched.
explainer: 'It is. Are you?' A brand new broadsheet with no proprietor.

question: TV-am launched breakfast television on ITV, with its 'Famous Five' presenters.
explainer: Then Roland Rat came along and saved the day.

question: Roxy Music released their glam debut single "Virginia Plain".
explainer: Bryan Ferry, feathers, and pure art-school cool.

question: British Leyland launched the Austin Allegro.
explainer: The square steering wheel was called the 'Quartic'. It did not catch on.

question: Channel 5 launched, opening with the Spice Girls.
explainer: First, millions of people had to retune their video recorders.

question: The world's first text message was sent, over the Vodafone network.
explainer: It said 'Merry Christmas'. Sent from a computer, as phones couldn't type yet.

question: The Pogues and Kirsty MacColl released "Fairytale of New York".
explainer: The best Christmas song never to reach number one.

question: BBC Radio 1 launched, with Tony Blackburn at the microphone.
explainer: The first record played was 'Flowers in the Rain' by The Move.

question: Aldi opened its first UK store, in Birmingham.
explainer: Stechford, of all places. Middle aisle madness had arrived.

question: Mr Blobby was the Christmas number one.
explainer: A big pink spotty blob beat Take That. Britain, explain yourself.

question: Soft Cell's "Tainted Love" topped the UK charts.
explainer: A Northern Soul cover reborn as the sound of synth-pop.

question: "Grease" was released.
explainer: Danny, Sandy, and a soundtrack that still fills every wedding dance floor.

question: Nokia launched the 3310 mobile phone.
explainer: Indestructible, a battery that lasted a week, and Snake II.

question: Loaded, the original 'lads' mag', was launched.
explainer: 'For men who should know better.' And mostly didn't.

question: Ernie Wise made the UK's first public mobile phone call.
explainer: On a phone the size of a house brick, on New Year's Day.

question: "Jurassic Park" was released.
explainer: Dinosaurs brought to life, and a glass of water that wobbled.

question: Anthony Joshua beat Wladimir Klitschko in front of 90,000 at Wembley.
explainer: A knockdown, a comeback, and one of the great heavyweight nights.

question: Domino's delivered its first pizza in the UK, from a shop in Luton.
explainer: A pizza at your door in thirty minutes was pure science fiction until then.

question: "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial" was released.
explainer: E.T. phone home. And a bike flying across the moon.

question: The free Metro newspaper was launched on the London Underground.
explainer: Read on the Tube, left on the seat, read by the next person.

question: The PG Tips chimps starred in their first TV advert.
explainer: Chimps having a tea party. It ran, in various forms, for decades.

question: Frank Bruno finally became world heavyweight champion, at Wembley.
explainer: 'Know what I mean, Harry?' Fourth time lucky.

question: Bryan Adams spent 16 weeks at number one with "(Everything I Do) I Do It for You".
explainer: Robin Hood's theme tune, all summer long. Everyone was quite sick of it.

question: "Inspector Morse" first aired, with John Thaw as the Oxford detective.
explainer: Crosswords, real ale, a maroon Jaguar and a great deal of Wagner.

question: Baileys Irish Cream went on sale.
explainer: Whiskey and cream in one bottle. Christmas drinks cabinets everywhere rejoiced.

question: Travis released the album "The Man Who".
explainer: 'Why Does It Always Rain on Me?' Post-Britpop melancholy, done beautifully.

question: The Sun ran its famous 'Gotcha' headline during the Falklands War.
explainer: Probably the most infamous front page in Fleet Street history.

question: Pizza Hut opened its first UK restaurant, in Islington.
explainer: Red roofs, the salad bar tower challenge, and birthday treats for a generation.

question: "Multi-Coloured Swap Shop", with Noel Edmonds, first aired.
explainer: Swapping your Action Man for a skateboard, live on BBC One.

question: Pot Noodle first went on sale.
explainer: Just add boiling water. And, for many, a small amount of shame.

question: Phil Collins released "In the Air Tonight".
explainer: That drum fill. You know the one. Everybody air-drums it.

question: Wall's launched Viennetta.
explainer: Ice cream with crunchy chocolate layers. The height of dinner-party sophistication.

question: Freeview launched, rising from the ashes of ITV Digital.
explainer: Digital telly with no subscription. And no knitted monkey.

question: Henry Cooper floored Muhammad Ali with a left hook known as 'Enry's 'Ammer.
explainer: Down went the great man, before a split glove bought him time to recover.

question: Rowntree's launched the Yorkie bar, aimed squarely at lorry drivers.
explainer: Chunky, manly, and later, rather unwisely, 'not for girls'.

question: "Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?" first aired, with Chris Tarrant.
explainer: Phone a friend, ask the audience, and 'is that your final answer?'

question: Chelsea won the Champions League for the first time, in Munich.
explainer: Didier Drogba, a header, and the winning penalty.

question: Private Eye published its first issue.
explainer: Lord Gnome's organ, and a great many lawsuits.

question: The world's first cash machine opened, outside Barclays in Enfield.
explainer: Reg Varney, of On the Buses, made the first withdrawal. Using a paper voucher.

question: Wallace and Gromit's "The Wrong Trousers" was first shown.
explainer: Techno trousers, a sinister penguin, and that train-track chase.

question: The Manchester Guardian dropped 'Manchester' from its name.
explainer: Plain old The Guardian from then on. The move to London came later.

question: Nick Kamen stripped to his boxers in the Levi's launderette advert.
explainer: Sales of 501s went through the roof. So did sales of boxer shorts.

question: "Doctor Who" returned to TV, with Christopher Eccleston as the Doctor.
explainer: Sixteen years off air, then straight back to Saturday-night glory.

question: The Austin Metro was launched, 'a British car to beat the world'.
explainer: Lady Diana drove one. Sales, briefly, were very good indeed.

question: James Hunt won the Formula One World Championship.
explainer: A playboy, a rival named Lauda, and a title settled in the Japanese rain.

question: "The X Factor" first aired.
explainer: Simon Cowell, sob stories, and a Christmas number one machine.

question: "Father Ted" first aired on Channel 4.
explainer: Craggy Island, Mrs Doyle, and 'down with this sort of thing'.

question: Barclaycard, Britain's first credit card, was launched.
explainer: Plastic money arrived, and spending what you didn't have became very easy indeed.

question: Manic Street Preachers released "A Design for Life".
explainer: Libraries gave us power, and Welsh rock one of its finest anthems.

question: KFC opened its first UK branch, in Preston.
explainer: The Colonel's secret recipe made its British debut in Lancashire.

question: Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells" became the very first Virgin Records release.
explainer: It started Richard Branson's empire. Then it scored The Exorcist.

question: "Spitting Image", the satirical puppet show, first appeared.
explainer: Grotesque latex politicians, and absolutely nobody spared.

question: The Shadows topped the charts with the instrumental "Apache".
explainer: Hank Marvin's twangy guitar, and a thousand bedroom guitarists born.

question: "Raiders of the Lost Ark" was released.
explainer: Indiana Jones, a giant boulder, and snakes. Why did it have to be snakes?

question: Dyson launched its first bagless vacuum cleaner, the DC01.
explainer: After more than 5,000 prototypes in a shed. Persistence, thy name is James.

question: "Gladiators" first aired on ITV.
explainer: Wolf, Jet, Lightning, and the dreaded Eliminator.

question: IKEA opened its first UK store, in Warrington.
explainer: Flat-pack furniture, meatballs, and the very first arguments over missing screws.

question: Suede released their self-titled debut album.
explainer: The band that lit the fuse for Britpop, all glamour and gloom.

question: "Star Wars" opened in British cinemas.
explainer: A long time ago, in a galaxy far, far away. Queues round the block.

question: Smash Hits magazine was first published.
explainer: Song lyrics, posters, and 'Black Type' for every pop fan.

question: Tamagotchi virtual pets arrived in Britain.
explainer: Feed it, clean it, and watch it die during double maths. Then get it confiscated.

question: Roald Dahl's "Charlie and the Chocolate Factory" was published.
explainer: Golden tickets, a chocolate river, and one very deserving boy.

question: Compare the Market launched its meerkat adverts.
explainer: Aleksandr Orlov, 'simples', and a cuddly toy in every other house.

question: "Dirty Dancing" was released.
explainer: Nobody puts Baby in a corner. That lift, in that lake.

question: Eddie 'the Eagle' Edwards ski-jumped for Britain at the Calgary Winter Olympics.
explainer: He came last. Everybody loved him anyway.

question: "Mastermind" first aired, with Magnus Magnusson.
explainer: 'I've started, so I'll finish.' The black chair was born.

question: Virgin Atlantic made its first flight, from Gatwick to Newark.
explainer: Richard Branson's record label took to the skies. As you do.

question: Katrina and the Waves won Eurovision with "Love Shine a Light".
explainer: The UK's fifth Eurovision win. Shine a light, indeed.

question: The Smash Martians adverts first appeared, laughing at humans peeling potatoes.
explainer: 'For mash get Smash.' Tin robots, cackling, forever.

question: Sally Gunnell won Olympic 400m hurdles gold in Barcelona.
explainer: Over the barriers and away. Britain's golden girl of the track.

question: Frankie Goes to Hollywood released "Relax", which the BBC promptly banned.
explainer: The ban, naturally, sent it straight to number one.

question: Opal Fruits were renamed Starburst.
explainer: Made to make your mouth water. And your nan still calls them Opal Fruits.

question: The News of the World published its final edition.
explainer: Closed after 168 years, in the middle of the phone-hacking scandal.

question: "Skyfall", the James Bond film, was released.
explainer: Adele's theme, the Aston Martin, and Judi Dench's farewell as M.

question: Amstrad launched its CPC 464 home computer, with a built-in tape deck.
explainer: Alan Sugar's all-in-one. Plug it in and wait ten minutes for a game to load.

question: "Red Dwarf", the sci-fi sitcom, first aired.
explainer: Three million years into deep space, with a curry and a hologram.
